extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of aesthetic criticism, art and literary critics, and educated general readers interested in critique of art and poetry
extracted.subtask_short: aesthetic criticism of art and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for practising close aesthetic criticism of visual art and poetry: how to perceive, analyse, and describe what produces pleasure in a work, and how to separate its central artistic virtues from adjuncts, historical context, or debris.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete, particular definition of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not seek an abstract universal formula for beauty; define beauty in the most concrete terms possible for each special manifestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The value of abstract definitions is limited; the critic's aim is "not a universal formula for it, but the formula which expresses most adequately this or that special manifestation of it." Anti-pattern: attempting to judge works by an abstract, one-size-fits-all definition of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: See the object as it really is
rubrics_metrics.description: "To see the object as in itself it really is" is the aim of true criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting theories or metaphysical questions override direct apprehension of the work. Treat the work on its own terms rather than subordinating it to abstract systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and discriminate one's own impression
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step in aesthetic criticism is to know one's own impression as it really is: to discriminate it and realise it distinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the primary questions the author gives: What effect does it produce on me? Does it give me pleasure, and if so what sort or degree? How is my nature modified by its presence? Treat these felt impressions as the original facts for criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regard works as powers producing unique pleasurable sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Regard pictures, poems, and accomplished forms of life as receptacles of many powers that produce pleasurable sensations, each of a peculiar, unique kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse the particular kind of pleasure produced and reduce the influence to its elements. This frames evaluation around the specific sensory/emotional effects a work yields, rather than general evaluative labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolate the 'virtue' or active principle responsible for pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish, analyse, and separate from its adjuncts the virtue by which a work produces its special impression of beauty or pleasure; indicate the source of that impression and the conditions under which it is experienced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic's end is reached when he has disengaged that virtue and noted it 'as a chemist notes some natural element.' Practical step: identify the single quality or active principle in a work (e.g., Wordsworth's mystical sense of life in nature) and show how it operates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate temperament and susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess a certain kind of temperament — the power of being deeply moved by the presence of beautiful objects — rather than merely an abstract intellectual definition of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education in criticism advances as one's susceptibility to impressions increases in depth and variety. The critic must be an 'exquisite amateur' who feels strongly and can analyse feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pluralism across periods, schools, and types
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that beauty exists in many forms; to the critic all periods, types, and schools of taste are in themselves equal — genius stands above its age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid chronocentric or school-based prejudice. The central question: 'In whom did the stir, the genius, the sentiment of the period find itself?' Focus on exemplars rather than ranking periods as inherently superior or inferior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disentangle core virtues from debris/adjuncts
rubrics_metrics.description: Many artists' works combine brilliant 'virtue' with commoner elements; the critic must have the nicety to disengage the virtue from its adjuncts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Wordsworth contains crystallised parts and much that might be forgotten; the critic should follow where the active principle penetrates and mark its degree. Anti-pattern: taking an artist's entire oeuvre as uniformly representative without separating stronger from weaker parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require intrinsic aesthetic quality before valuing antiquarian/contextual interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical or antiquarian interest can enhance appreciation only if the work possesses a real, direct aesthetic charm in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antiquarian perspective may put past pleasures in perspective, but cannot impart aesthetic value where none originally existed. Practical implication: do not let historical curiosity substitute for intrinsic artistic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value manner and form as much as matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner (form, style, presentation) of a work is central to its aesthetic effect; a tragic subject may be shaped into something of joy by manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Aucassin and Nicolette treats a sorrowful subject yet claims to be 'a thing of joy and refreshment' through its manner. Evaluate how form and treatment transform subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to concrete details and recurring objects that sustain sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete details and recurring beautiful objects (tokens, props) keep sensation awake and give refinement and a feeling of fate to narrative or poetic scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the two identical cups in Amis and Amile, Othello's handkerchief. In criticism and creation, note how material details sustain reader/listener sensation and contribute to meaning and mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider performative, musical, and medium-specific aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium and performative context (recitation, song, music, staging) are part of the artistic effect and must be considered in evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Aucassin and Nicolette's inserted songs (cantefable) and possible dramatic action shape its effect; new poetic music (approach to rhyme) is itself a criterion of interest. When assessing a work, attend to how it would be experienced in performance.
